hero.prompt: A friendly flat cartoon of a sunny Rift Valley maize farm: rows of tall green maize plants, a wooden farm gate, a round water tank on a stand, a small shed with solar panels on its roof and a green escarpment behind.
hero.alt: A drawing of a maize farm in the Rift Valley with maize rows, a gate, a water tank and solar panels on a shed.

slides.title: Your brain's first draft
slides.subtitle: Work alone and in silence. Write what you think. Then we talk.

blocks.text: A school desk with a blank sheet showing one large empty rounded outline, a pencil, a green pen and a red pen.
items: desk_plant_cell_outline_sheet
A friendly flat cartoon of a wooden classroom desk holding a blank sheet of paper with one large empty rounded outline, a pencil, a green pen and a red pen, with sunlight from a window.

blocks.text: Which organelles does a plant cell have? Which does it share with an animal cell?

items: pencil :: Write every organelle you think a plant cell has
star :: Put a ★ next to any you think an animal cell also has

do: Give each student a blank plant cell outline (photocopy, or draw one on the board for students to copy).
Say the words below, then start the 4-minute timer.
Stay at the front for the 4 minutes. Do not walk around yet.
Scan from the front for sheets with no writing.
say: Before I show you anything, I want your brain's first draft. Write every organelle you think a plant cell has. Put a star next to any you think it shares with the animal cell we studied last lesson.
notes.wait_time: 4 minutes of silent writing. Stay silent yourself.
look_for: Every student has at least 3 organelles written before the partner talk.
Note any student with a blank sheet for support.
if_then: If a sheet is blank when the timer ends, say quietly: 'Write one thing you remember about cells. A guess is fine.'
If a student asks 'Is this right?', say: 'This is your first draft. We will check it together later.'
notes.why_this_works: Students commit to an idea before any teaching. This makes the new learning something to confirm or correct, not something to just receive.
answer_key: Any honest list is accepted. Example: cell wall, nucleus ★, chloroplast, vacuole, mitochondria ★, cell membrane ★.

slides.title: Compare with your partner
slides.subtitle: Talk about your lists. Listen to each other's reasons.

items: people :: Turn to your shoulder partner
thought :: Compare your lists
question :: Do you agree on which organelles are shared?

do: Students turn to a shoulder partner. Pairs only.
Start the 2-minute timer.
Now you may walk around and listen. Do not correct.
say: Turn to your partner. Compare your lists. Do you agree on which organelles are shared?
look_for: Both partners speak.
Pairs who disagree about the stars. Remember them for the cold-call.
if_then: If a pair finishes early, say: 'Tell your partner WHY you put each star.'
If a pair has nothing to say, say: 'Pick one organelle you are sure about. Tell your partner why.'
notes.why_this_works: Saying an idea aloud to one partner is low risk. It lets every student rehearse before speaking to the whole class.

slides.title: BEFORE — Our Predictions
slides.subtitle: Hands up. We write all ideas on the board. No corrections yet.

items: raised_hand :: Hands up if you predicted chloroplasts
raised_hand :: Keep it up if you marked chloroplasts as shared with animal cells
SHARED :: Organelles we think plant and animal cells share
PLANT ONLY :: Organelles we think only plant cells have

do: Run the show-of-hands poll. Count the hands each time and write both counts on the board.
Draw two columns on the board: SHARED and PLANT ONLY. Title: BEFORE — Our Predictions.
Cold-call 3 students who kept their hand up for chloroplasts being shared.
Write class predictions in the two columns. Leave the board visible all lesson.
say: Hands up if you predicted chloroplasts.
Keep your hand up if you also marked chloroplasts as shared with animal cells.
Akinyi, why did you think animal cells also have chloroplasts?
Thank you. That is a prediction. We will come back to it with evidence.
notes.wait_time: 12 seconds after each cold-call question, before taking an answer
look_for: Count how many hands stay up. If more than 40% of the class, note it: you must address chloroplasts clearly in Explain.
Choose students to cold-call who kept their hand up. They give the clearest view of the misconception.
Check that the board has at least 5 different organelles listed.
if_then: If a student says all cells have chloroplasts, say: 'Thank you. We will test that idea with evidence.' Do not correct yet.
If nobody keeps a hand up, ask: 'What did the people who wrote chloroplast think the cell does with sunlight?'
notes.why_this_works: A visible mismatch in raised hands shows the class a real puzzle. The two-column board gives them a target to confirm or revise. The common misconception is that every cell has chloroplasts.

slides.title: Look first. Do not write yet.
slides.subtitle: Notice what is familiar from the animal cell lesson. Notice what is new.
slides.time_note: 90 seconds of silent looking, plus set-up

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.

do: Show the fully labelled plant cell diagram. Project it or post the large printed copy at the front.
Start the 90-second timer.
Students look only. No pens.
say: You have 90 seconds to look — do not write yet. Just look. Notice what is familiar from our animal cell lesson and what is completely new.
look_for: Pens are down and eyes are on the diagram.
if_then: If students start writing, say: 'Pens down. Just look for now.'
notes.why_this_works: Looking before writing means students write what they actually saw. They do not write whatever comes to mind first.

slides.title: Electron micrographs
slides.subtitle: Real images made with electrons, not light. Look silently at each one.
slides.time_note: 60 seconds for each image (where a projector is available)

items: leaf :: 1. A chloroplast from a maize leaf
onion :: 2. A large central vacuole in an onion epidermal cell
magnifier :: 3. The cell wall between two plant cells

do: Where a projector is available, show the three electron micrographs one at a time, 60 seconds each.
Keep the projector power cable secured and away from the walkways.
Say the line below before the first image.
No projector? Skip this slide and give the 3 minutes to the annotation slide.
say: This is an actual electron micrograph — a photograph taken with a beam of electrons, not light. The chloroplast you are looking at is from a maize leaf, the same maize grown in farms around the Rift Valley.
notes.wait_time: 60 seconds of silence for each image
look_for: Students look closely and stay silent.
Students point out things that match the labelled diagram.
if_then: If students ask what a part is, say: 'Keep looking. You will label it in a moment.'
If the images do not load, say: 'Use the labelled diagram. It shows the same parts.'
notes.why_this_works: Real images show students that the drawings come from real cells. Silent looking builds careful observation.

slides.title: Annotate your outline
slides.subtitle: Label each organelle. Add one short function phrase in your own words.

blocks.text: Label each organelle. Beside each label write what it does.
items: Example: chloroplast — captures sunlight to make food

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.

do: Students work alone on their blank outline from Predict.
Keep the labelled diagram on view.
Start the 8-minute timer.
Walk around and read as they write. Do NOT correct yet.
Choose 5 random sheets and collect them for a quick scan before Explain.
say: Now annotate your outline. For every organelle you label, write a short function phrase — one line, in your own words.
look_for: Each sheet has a label AND a function phrase for at least 7 of the 9 organelles. Check 5 or 6 sheets while you walk.
Students write function phrases, not just names.
if_then: If a student has only labels, say: 'Good. Now beside each label write what it does. Use your own words.'
If the 5 collected sheets show fewer than 5 of 9 function phrases, pause at the start of Explain and model two or three phrases on the board.
notes.why_this_works: Adding a function phrase makes students link each part to a job. A name alone is easy to copy and forget.
answer_key: Model function phrases: cell wall — gives shape, support and protection; cell membrane — controls what enters and leaves; nucleus — holds the DNA and gives instructions; chloroplast — captures sunlight to make food (glucose) by photosynthesis; large central vacuole — stores water, keeps pressure (turgor), stores nutrients and waste; mitochondria — release energy from glucose (respiration); endoplasmic reticulum — transports and modifies proteins made by ribosomes; ribosomes — build proteins; Golgi apparatus — sorts, modifies and ships proteins and lipids.

slides.title: Peer check
slides.subtitle: Swap sheets with your partner. Check the labels and function notes.

items: pencil :: Swap sheets with your partner
check :: Tick what matches the diagram
pencil :: Add a correction in a different colour pen

do: Pairs swap sheets. Each uses a green or red pen.
Show the labelled diagram again, or keep the poster up.
Start the 4-minute timer.
Walk around and listen.
say: Swap sheets with your partner. Using your green or red pen, tick what matches the diagram and add a correction where needed.
look_for: Corrections are in a different colour from the first writing.
Check 5 or 6 sheets. Corrections are polite and based on the diagram.
if_then: If a pair has no corrections, say: 'Look at the vacuole and the ER again. Is each function note complete?'
If a student argues, say: 'Check the diagram. What does it show?'
notes.why_this_works: A different colour makes revision visible and not shameful. Students learn to check ideas against evidence.
answer_key: Example: Partner wrote 'mitochondria — makes food'. Peer corrects in red pen: 'mitochondria — release energy from glucose'.

slides.title: Our maize farm in the Rift Valley
slides.subtitle: Every organelle has a farming job.

blocks.text: A drawing of a maize farm in the Rift Valley with maize rows, a gate, a water tank and solar panels on a shed.
items: rift_valley_maize_farm

A friendly flat cartoon of a sunny Rift Valley maize farm: rows of tall green maize plants, a wooden farm gate, a round water tank on a stand, a small shed with solar panels on its roof and a green escarpment behind.
eyes :: Look at the organelle on the diagram
speech :: Finish: 'In our maize farm, this organelle is like the … because …'
pencil :: Check the board and add what you missed

blocks.text: Keep your first prediction list and a different colour pen.

do: Collect or check the 5 sheets from Observe. If fewer than 5 of 9 organelles have function phrases, model 2 or 3 phrases on the board now.
Draw an empty table on the board: ORGANELLE, FARM JOB, FUNCTION. Fill it one line at a time.
Tell students the 3-step routine on the slide. You will use it for each of the 9 organelles.
say: Now we build the explanation together. Think of a maize farm in the Rift Valley. Every part of the farm has a job. Every part of the cell has a job too.
For each organelle I will ask you to finish a sentence. Think first. I will call on someone.
look_for: Students have their prediction lists and a different colour pen ready.
if_then: If students are unsure about the farm, say: 'Think of a maize farm you know. What does it need to grow maize?'
notes.why_this_works: A familiar farm gives students a picture to hang each new word on. Asking them to guess the link before you confirm keeps them thinking during teaching. The farm only works if students also know where it stops: it is a comparison, not the real cell.
notes.science_note: The farm is an analogy. A cell is not a farm. Farm parts are bigger, fixed and made of different material. Use the farm to help memory, then use the diagram for the real structure.

slides.title: Farm jobs 1: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus
slides.subtitle: Finish the sentence for each organelle.
slides.time_note: About 2 minutes for each organelle, with 12 seconds of wait time

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.
In our maize farm, this organelle is like the … because …

do: Point to the cell wall. Say the sentence starter. Wait 12 seconds. Cold-call one student to finish it. Confirm. Write the farm job and function on the board.
Repeat for the cell membrane, then the nucleus.
Choose a different student each time. Choose one who has not spoken yet and one who was unsure in the peer check.
say: In our maize farm, this cell wall is like the … because …
In our maize farm, this cell membrane is like the … because …
In our maize farm, this nucleus is like the … because …
notes.wait_time: 12 seconds after each question, before you call on anyone
look_for: Each of the 3 students you call links the farm job to the function and gives a reason with 'because'.
Students do not mix up the cell wall and the cell membrane.
if_then: If a student guesses a wrong job, say: 'Good thinking. What does the cell wall do? Which part of the farm does that job?'
If students say the wall and the membrane are the same thing, say: 'Look at the diagram. Which one is outside? A fence is outside. A gate lets things in and out.'
notes.why_this_works: Students predict the link before you confirm it. This keeps them thinking during teaching. It also shows the wall and the membrane do different jobs.
answer_key: Cell wall — the perimeter fence and brick walls of the farm: gives shape, support and protection.
Cell membrane — the farm gate: controls what enters and leaves.
Nucleus — the farm owner's office: holds all the plans (DNA) and gives instructions.

slides.title: Farm jobs 2: chloroplast, vacuole, mitochondria
slides.subtitle: Finish the sentence for each organelle.
slides.time_note: About 2 minutes for each organelle, with 12 seconds of wait time

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.
In our maize farm, this organelle is like the … because …

do: Point to the chloroplast. Say the sentence starter. Wait 12 seconds. Cold-call one student. Confirm. Write on the board.
Repeat for the large central vacuole, then the mitochondria.
For the chloroplast, remind the class of the hands-up poll from Predict.
Choose one student who kept their hand up for 'chloroplast shared' and one who did not.
say: In our maize farm, this chloroplast is like the … because …
In our maize farm, this large central vacuole is like the … because …
In our maize farm, these mitochondria are like the … because …
notes.wait_time: 12 seconds after each question, before you call on anyone
look_for: Each of the 3 students you call gives a farm job and a function with 'because'.
Students keep the chloroplast (makes food) and the mitochondria (release energy) separate.
if_then: If a student mixes up chloroplast and mitochondria, say: 'One captures sunlight to make food. One releases energy from that food. Which is which?'
If a student says plants only have chloroplasts, say: 'Plants need energy from glucose too. Which organelle releases it?'
notes.why_this_works: Chloroplasts and mitochondria are often mixed up. Asking students to guess the farm job first shows who has the idea and who needs help.
answer_key: Chloroplast — the solar panels on the farm: capture sunlight to make food (glucose) by photosynthesis.
Large central vacuole — the farm's water storage tank: stores water, keeps pressure (turgor), stores nutrients and waste.
Mitochondria — the farm's generator: release energy from glucose for all farm activities (respiration).
notes.science_note: Plant cells have mitochondria as well as chloroplasts. Chloroplasts make glucose. Mitochondria release energy from it.

slides.title: Farm jobs 3: ER, ribosomes, Golgi apparatus
slides.subtitle: Finish the sentence for each organelle.
slides.time_note: About 2 minutes for each organelle, with 12 seconds of wait time

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.
In our maize farm, this organelle is like the … because …

do: Point to the endoplasmic reticulum (the table says rough ER). Say the sentence starter. Wait 12 seconds. Cold-call one student. Confirm. Write on the board.
Repeat for the ribosomes, then the Golgi apparatus.
That makes 9 cold-calls across the table. Use 9 different students if you can.
Ribosomes and Golgi are often mixed up. Ask, 'Who makes?' and 'Who ships?'
say: In our maize farm, this endoplasmic reticulum is like the … because …
In our maize farm, these ribosomes are like the … because …
In our maize farm, this Golgi apparatus is like the … because …
notes.wait_time: 12 seconds after each question, before you call on anyone
look_for: Each of the 3 students you call gives a farm job and a function with 'because'.
Students say that ribosomes build proteins and that the Golgi sorts and ships them.
if_then: If a student says the Golgi makes proteins, say: 'Who builds the proteins on our farm? Who packs and sends them out?'
If students are lost, say: 'Look at the board. Which line is the delivery road? Which is the depot?'
notes.why_this_works: Making and dispatching are easy to mix up. The farm picture of workers and depot gives two separate jobs. The cold-call shows if the idea stuck.
answer_key: Rough endoplasmic reticulum — the farm's delivery road network with loading bays: transports and modifies proteins made by ribosomes.
Ribosomes — the farm workers: build proteins from instructions sent by the nucleus.
Golgi apparatus — the farm's packaging and dispatch depot: sorts, modifies and ships proteins and lipids to where they are needed.

slides.title: Right or wrong? Check your predictions
slides.subtitle: Go back to your first draft from the start of the lesson.

items: pencil :: Use a pen in a different colour
check :: Tick (✓) each organelle that a plant cell really has
cross :: Put ✗ by any that were wrong
question :: Not sure about a ★? Write ? for now

do: Point to the BEFORE — Our Predictions board. Students mark their own lists.
Walk around and look at 5 or 6 sheets.
Use the board table the class built, with all nine organelles.
say: Look at your first draft. Use a different colour pen. Tick what you got right. Put a cross by what was wrong. If you are not sure about a star, write a question mark. We will come back to it.
look_for: Marks are in a different colour pen.
Students mark their own work, including the things they got wrong. Check 5 or 6 sheets.
if_then: If a student feels bad about ✗ marks, say: 'A cross means you found something new. That is good science.'
If a student ticks everything, say: 'Check each organelle against the board table. Did you really have it?'
notes.why_this_works: Marking a prediction in a new colour shows students how their ideas changed. It makes self-correction normal.
answer_key: Plant cells have all nine organelles on the board. Model marking: a student who wrote 'chloroplast' puts ✓. A student who wrote 'lysosome' puts ✗ because it is not in the nine.

Stars: cell membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes and Golgi apparatus are shared with animal cells. Cell wall, chloroplast and large central vacuole are plant only. Students settle the chloroplast star after the triad talk.

slides.title: Organelle Job Card
slides.subtitle: Write the organelle for each farm job. Work alone.

items: The farm's water storage tank
The farm gate
The farm's generator
The perimeter fence and brick walls
The farm owner's office
The farm's packaging and dispatch depot
The solar panels on the farm
The farm workers
The delivery roads with loading bays

do: Give out the Organelle Job Card: a half-page with two columns, ORGANELLE and FARM JOB. Farm jobs are listed. Organelles are blank.
Students work alone for 4 minutes.
Collect all the cards at the end.
Mark them later. Learners with 5 or fewer correct need a quick re-teach. Pull them aside during Model Building.
say: Write the organelle for each farm job. Work alone. You have 4 minutes.
look_for: Each card has at least 8 of 9 correct matches. Check 6 cards quickly while students write.
Common mix-ups: ribosomes and Golgi; chloroplast and mitochondria.
if_then: If a student is stuck, say: 'Look at the board table. Find the farm job. Read across to the organelle.'
If many students score 5 or fewer, say to the class: 'Let us look at the board again. Which job is the farm worker?'
notes.why_this_works: Matching from memory shows who has the idea and who copied. The cards give you the data to plan the re-teach.
answer_key: The farm's water storage tank — large central vacuole.
The farm gate — cell membrane.
The farm's generator — mitochondria.
The perimeter fence and brick walls — cell wall.
The farm owner's office — nucleus.
The farm's packaging and dispatch depot — Golgi apparatus.
The solar panels on the farm — chloroplast.
The farm workers — ribosomes.
The delivery roads with loading bays — endoplasmic reticulum (rough).

slides.title: Why no chloroplasts in Amina's skin cells?
slides.subtitle: Plant cells have chloroplasts. The skin cells that healed her finger do not.

blocks.text: A girl smiling and holding up one finger with a neat plaster on it, beside a chopping board with sliced onions.
items: amina_healing_finger

A friendly flat cartoon of one teenage girl in a school uniform smiling and holding up one hand with a neat plaster on her finger, standing beside a kitchen table with a wooden chopping board of sliced onions.

blocks.text: Why do Amina's skin cells have no chloroplasts? What does that tell us?
Talk in groups of three. Use these starters.
items: Skin cells have no chloroplasts because …
This tells us that a cell's structure is linked to its …

do: Students sit in groups of three (triads) and talk for 2 minutes.
Ask the question. Wait 15 seconds. Then let triads talk.
Listen to 2 triads. Then cold-call 2 students, one from each of the triads you listened to.
Go back to the BEFORE — Our Predictions board. Ask students to fix their chloroplast star now, in the different colour pen.
say: Think back to Amina's cut finger. The epidermal cells that grew back over the wound are animal cells. They have no chloroplasts. Why not? What does that tell you?
This is the heart of our driving question. Every organelle exists because the cell's job demands it. No more, no less.
notes.wait_time: 15 seconds after the question, before triads talk
look_for: Listen to 2 triads. Do they use the phrase 'structure matches function', or an idea like it, in their own words?
Students say skin cells do not make food, so they do not need chloroplasts.
if_then: If a triad says 'they just don't have them', ask: 'What does a chloroplast DO? Where do skin cells get their energy?'
If students say cells lose chloroplasts when they are hurt, say: 'Skin cells never had chloroplasts. Think about the job of skin cells.'
notes.why_this_works: Going straight back to the cut finger turns the farm picture into a tool for reasoning. Structure and job are linked. The common idea that all cells have chloroplasts is tested against the cells students already know.
answer_key: Skin cells have no chloroplasts because they do not make their own food by photosynthesis. They get energy from food, so a chloroplast would be wasteful. This tells us that a cell's structure is linked to its job: structure matches function.

slides.title: Driving Question Board: write your note
slides.subtitle: One sticky note each. Work alone and in silence.

blocks.text: A classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes with small gold stars beside some of them.
items: dqb_sticky_notes_board
A friendly flat cartoon of a classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes, with three small gold stars stuck beside some notes, and a wooden desk with a pot of pencils in front.
Row A :: What does today's lesson about plant cell organelles help you understand about the driving question — why do cells look different?
Row B :: What new question does today's lesson raise for you about cell structure or the healing cut?

do: Give each student a sticky note, or a folded card if there are no sticky notes.
Row A answers the Row A prompt. Row B answers the Row B prompt.
Silent individual writing for 3 minutes.
Scan notes as students write.
say: You have 3 minutes — individual, silent. Write your best thinking on the prompt for your row.
look_for: Every student writes a note. Check the notes of at least 6 students.
Notes use something seen today, such as the diagram or the electron micrographs, and link to the driving question.
if_then: If a note only states a fact, such as 'chloroplasts do photosynthesis', ask: 'How does knowing that help explain why Amina's skin cells look different from a leaf cell?'
If a student is stuck, say: 'Think of one thing you saw today. What does it help you explain?'
notes.why_this_works: Writing a note makes each student take part in building the class answer. The board shows what the class knows and what it still wonders. A common mistake is treating the board as a vocabulary list.
answer_key: Row A model note: 'Plant cells have chloroplasts to make their own food. Amina's skin cells do not need them. Cells look different because their jobs are different.'
Row B model note: 'If skin cells have no chloroplasts, how do the cells that heal a cut get their energy?'

slides.title: Driving Question Board: post, read and vote
slides.subtitle: Post your note in the LESSON 4 section. Listen. Vote.
slides.time_note: Posting, 4 notes read aloud, class vote

items: pushpin :: Post your note in the LESSON 4 section
megaphone :: Listen as 4 notes are read aloud
check :: Thumbs up: growing understanding
question :: Question mark: new mystery

do: Students post their notes in the LESSON 4 section of the Driving Question Board.
Read 4 notes aloud: 2 from Row A and 2 from Row B.
After each note, ask the class to vote with a thumbs up or a question-mark gesture. Everyone votes.
Draw a line on the board between two notes that together suggest an answer.
say: Is this a growing understanding — something we are beginning to explain? Or is this a new mystery we still need to investigate?
We are building an answer — slowly, piece by piece, just like the cells rebuilding Amina's finger.
Plant cells have chloroplasts because they make their own food. Animal cells, including Amina's epidermal cells, do not need to.
notes.wait_time: 5 seconds after each note before the vote
look_for: Everyone votes. Look at all hands for each note.
Students can say why a note is understanding or a mystery. Ask 2 students to explain their vote.
Notes are based on what was seen or learned today, not copied from a book.
if_then: If the votes split, say: 'Some of you think it is understanding and some a mystery. What evidence do we have from today?'
If a note is off topic, say: 'That is interesting. How does it link to why cells look different?'
notes.why_this_works: Sorting notes into 'growing understanding' and 'new mystery' shows that science is built step by step. The line between notes shows how ideas from different lessons join into an answer.

slides.title: Model Building: Version 2 — The Plant Cell
slides.subtitle: Open your book to the page facing your cell model. Draw a plant cell.

items: pencil :: Draw the plant cell large, filling the page
pushpin :: Label all nine organelles
maize :: Write its farm job in brackets beside each label
palette :: Finished early? Green = plant only. Blue = shared

do: Students open their exercise book to their cumulative cell model (Version 1) and use the facing page for Version 2.
Students use their annotated outline and the board diagram as references.
Walk around and check three things: is the cell wall outside the cell membrane? Is the vacuole large and in the centre? Are the chloroplasts oval structures inside the cell?
Collect 6 books to mark overnight: two from each seating cluster.
Pull aside any learner with 5 or fewer correct on the Job Card for a quick re-teach.
say: Version 2 starts now. Open to the page facing your animal cell model. You are going to draw your plant cell large enough to fill the full page. We need room for all nine organelles and their farm labels.
look_for: Version 2 shows the cell wall outside the cell membrane, a large central vacuole, chloroplasts, and all 9 labels with farm jobs in brackets. Check 6 books.
Students do not copy without thinking.
if_then: If a drawing has an error, crouch beside the student and ask: 'Look at the diagram or the micrograph on the board. Where is the vacuole compared with the membrane?' Do not correct it for them.
If a student finishes early, say: 'Add colour: green for organelles only in plant cells, blue for organelles shared with animal cells.'
notes.why_this_works: Drawing Version 2 next to Version 1 lets students see how their model has grown. Writing the farm job in brackets joins the lesson's picture to the science. Students often draw the cell wall inside the membrane. Asking a question works better than telling them.
answer_key: A full-page plant cell with the cell wall outside the cell membrane, a large central vacuole, oval chloroplasts, and a nucleus, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes and Golgi apparatus. Each label has its farm job in brackets, for example: chloroplast (solar panels); large central vacuole (water storage tank).

slides.title: Two sentences for Version 2
slides.subtitle: Write them in the top corner of your Version 2 diagram.

blocks.text: Write two sentences.
items: 1. The biggest difference between Version 1 and Version 2 is …
2. This tells me that plant cells …
This is based on evidence from …

do: Say the line below. Students pause their drawing and write both sentences in the top corner.
They can finish the diagram afterwards.
Ask 2 volunteers to read their sentences aloud. Give short feedback.
say: Pause your drawing. Write your two sentences in the top corner now. You can finish the diagram after.
look_for: At least one of the two sentences names the chloroplast or the vacuole as a plant-unique feature. Check at least 6 books.
Sentence 2 says what the feature tells us about the plant cell's job.
Students name evidence they used.
if_then: If a student writes only 'plants have more parts', ask: 'Which parts? What job does each do?'
If a sentence does not link structure to function, say: 'Why would a plant cell need a chloroplast? Write that in your second sentence.'
notes.why_this_works: Writing the difference makes students put ideas together and not only copy. Naming the evidence shows the model comes from what they saw.
answer_key: The biggest difference between Version 1 and Version 2 is that the plant cell has a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole. This tells me that plant cells make their own food and keep water pressure to stay firm. This is based on evidence from the labelled diagram and the electron micrographs.

slides.title: Your prediction for Lesson 5
slides.subtitle: Your model now has two versions. Keep every version.

blocks.text: In Lesson 5 we compare plant and animal cells side by side. What do you predict we will find?
Write one sentence in your book.

do: Students write one sentence in their book.
Close the lesson with the words below.
say: Your model now has two versions. In Lesson 5, we compare them side-by-side to answer a key part of our driving question. Hold onto every version. Your model is your growing understanding made visible.
look_for: Each sentence is a prediction with a reason. Read 3 or 4 as students write.
if_then: If a student writes 'I don't know', say: 'Make a best guess. What could be different between a leaf cell and a skin cell?'
notes.why_this_works: A prediction for the next lesson links today's learning to the next step. It keeps the driving question alive.
answer_key: I predict animal cells will have no chloroplasts, because they do not make their own food.

lesson_oneliner: Every part of a plant cell has a farming job.
purpose: Students identify nine plant cell organelles and describe what each one does, using labelled diagrams and electron micrographs.
Students use a Rift Valley maize farm as a comparison to remember each job. They also learn where the comparison stops.
Students link structure to function and return to the healing cut: why do the skin cells that healed Amina's finger have no chloroplasts?
Students build Version 2 of their cumulative cell model: the plant cell.
before_class: Photocopy one blank plant cell outline for each student, or plan to draw one on the board.
Print or prepare a large labelled plant cell diagram. Keep it hidden until after the predictions.
Prepare one Organelle Job Card per student: two columns, ORGANELLE and FARM JOB, with all farm jobs listed and the organelle column blank.
Check the projector and the three electron micrographs (maize chloroplast, onion vacuole, cell wall boundary). Secure the power cable away from walkways.
Get sticky notes or folded cards for the Driving Question Board. Make a LESSON 4 section on the board.
Decide Row A and Row B for the Driving Question Board prompts.
Make sure students have green or red pens and their books with Version 1 of the cell model.
Have chalk or markers ready for the SHARED / PLANT ONLY columns and the farm table.
do_not_show: Do not show the labelled plant cell diagram (slides 'Look first. Do not write yet.' and 'Annotate your outline') until students have written their predictions and the BEFORE board record is done.
Do not show the electron micrographs until after the labelled diagram has been viewed.
Do not write any farm job on the board until a student has tried to finish the sentence for that organelle.
Do not open the ARES readings or videos with students before they have finished annotating and the Explain phase is complete.
so_far: You have met the healing cut, learned what a cell is, and compared bacteria with cheek cells.
goals: Describe the job of nine parts of a plant cell.
Explain how a cell's structure matches its job.
Describe how your cell model changes when a plant cell is added.

key_words.definition: A small part inside a cell that has its own job.
The shape and parts of something.
Describing one thing as another to help us understand it.
A drawing or idea that shows how something works.
A very close-up picture made with electrons, not light.

resource_notes.note: Compares plant and animal cells, so it gives away the Predict answers. Use after the slide 'Right or wrong? Check your predictions', or in Lesson 5, which compares the two.
Plant vs animal exercise would reveal the shared and plant-only answers early. Use as practice after 'Organelle Job Card', or in Lesson 5's comparison.
Organelle overview fits Observe, but narration may explain functions before students annotate. Check that it is eukaryotic and not animal-only. Safer after Explain.
Plant cell structures reading suits the topic. Check the reading level for Grade 10 and that it does not give functions before annotation.
Overview of animal and plant cells matches Explain, but it also covers animal cells, which Lesson 5 compares. Check it keeps to the nine organelles.
Plant cell structure practice suits consolidation after the farm-metaphor explanation. Use after 'Organelle Job Card' for extra practice.

summary.observe_prompt: Describe the labelled plant cell diagram and the electron micrographs you looked at.
summary.learn_prompt: Name the nine plant cell organelles. Say what each one does.
summary.explain_prompt: Why do plant cells have chloroplasts and a large vacuole, but Amina's skin cells do not?
summary.next_lesson: We compare plant and animal cells side by side.
summary.answer_observe: I saw a fully labelled plant cell diagram. Where available, I also saw electron micrographs of a maize leaf chloroplast, a large central vacuole in an onion cell, and the cell wall boundary between two plant cells.
summary.answer_learn: Plant cells contain nine key organelles: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus, chloroplasts, large central vacuole, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes and Golgi apparatus. Each has a function linked to its structure. On the maize farm they are the fence, gate, office, solar panels, water tank, generator, delivery roads, workers and dispatch depot.
summary.answer_explain: Unlike the animal cells (such as epidermal cells and platelets) that healed Amina's cut, plant cells have chloroplasts and a large central vacuole. These match their job: making their own food and keeping the cell firm with water pressure. Skin cells do not make food, so they have no chloroplasts. Structure and function go together, as with the specialised cells in the wound-healing phenomenon.
reflection: Did the Rift Valley maize farm help students remember each function, or did it oversimplify any organelle?
Look at the Job Cards. Which mix-ups are common, for example ribosomes and Golgi apparatus, or chloroplast and mitochondria?
Did the Driving Question Board notes link to the driving question, or did students treat the board as a vocabulary list?
In the 6 books you collected, is the cell wall drawn outside the cell membrane, with a large central vacuole?
If fewer than 70% of students finished Version 2 with all 9 organelles, plan 5 minutes at the start of Lesson 5 for model completion.

unit_map_notes.why_this_works: A short look at the whole unit shows students where today fits. Returning to the driving question each lesson keeps the healing cut in their minds.
